title: Acts Axes Cash Loads
subject: Evidence
stem: Mary operates a private “Acts & Axes” booth that sells scripture-engraved toy arks at summer fairs. She sues Stephen, her weekend cash-box clerk, for taking booth receipts. Before the records evidence is offered, Stephen testifies that Mary paid him $3,200 for the season and that he never took any receipts. Mary calls a prepaid-card records custodian, who will testify that during that same season Stephen made $18,600 in cash loads onto his personal prepaid card. Stephen objects that the cash loads could have come from birthday gifts or family loans. The custodian’s testimony is:

choices.A: inadmissible, because financial records are always unfairly prejudicial in a civil theft case.
choices.B: admissible as circumstantial evidence that Stephen received funds from a source beyond his stated pay.
choices.C: inadmissible, because the cash loads do not conclusively prove Stephen took Mary’s receipts.
choices.D: admissible only to impeach Stephen, but not as circumstantial proof that he took the receipts.

rightExplanation: B is correct. The cash-load records are admissible because they make Mary’s claim more probable: Stephen said he received only $3,200 for the season, while the records show $18,600 in same-season cash loads. Gold Key: relevance is an “any tendency” threshold, not a conclusive-proof requirement. Silver Key: in a relevance array, cut answers that demand “conclusive,” “always,” or “only”; the surviving answer states what the evidence tends to show. Stephen may argue gifts or family loans, but that attacks weight, not admissibility.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: “Always unfairly prejudicial” is an absolute. Evidence prejudice is not automatic. Cut.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: “Conclusive proof” invents a threshold. The call is admissibility, not certainty. Cut.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: “Only to impeach” is too narrow. The records also tend to show funds beyond stated pay. Cut.

c3.label: Residual B
c3.text: B answers the call and states the evidence’s proper circumstantial use. No CLASH or CALL needed after the CUT.

studentScript: Pay $3,200, cash loads $18,600, denial. A says always, C says conclusive, D says only. B is the only answer that says what the records tend to show.

A.signal: The word 'always' turns a balancing idea into automatic exclusion.
A.lawyer: Rule 403 uses a substantial-outweighing balance; it is not an automatic exclusion for financial records.

B.signal: This answer matches the call and the fact gap: stated pay versus larger cash loads.
B.lawyer: The records satisfy the relevance threshold and are admissible absent a Rule 403 exclusion.

C.signal: The word 'conclusively' invents a higher admissibility threshold.
C.lawyer: Relevant evidence need not prove the fact by itself; weaknesses are for the factfinder.

D.signal: The word 'only' underclaims the evidence's purpose.
D.lawyer: The evidence can both contradict Stephen and serve as substantive circumstantial proof.

goldKeys.statement: Relevant evidence does not need to prove the whole case by itself. If it has any tendency to make a consequential fact more probable, it clears the relevance threshold.
goldKeys.trigger: The opponent says the evidence could have another explanation.
goldKeys.authority: Fed. R. Evid. 401, 402, 403; see pass-1 legal verification.

silverKeys.statement: In a relevance array, cut 'conclusive,' 'always,' and 'only' before weighing the story. The survivor usually states what the evidence tends to show.
silverKeys.trigger: Three choices narrow admissibility; one states the fact relation.

remediation.title: Relevance is a clue threshold
remediation.signal: Opponent says the evidence has innocent explanations or is not conclusive.
remediation.studentMove: Ask what fact the evidence tends to make more likely.
remediation.tinyRule: A clue need not be a confession.
